title: Asymmetric poletop
description: A poletop with an asymmetric arrangement of insulators/wires, seen around central Mexico (État de México, Hidalgo, Tlaxcala, Morelos, Puebla area per the guide's map).

title: Concrete pole with hanging insulators
description: Concrete pole with a double crossarm carrying insulators that visibly "hang" below the arm. Seen around the Gulf coast and Yucatán Peninsula (Veracruz, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán, Quintana Roo).

title: Wooden pole with hanging insulators
description: Wooden pole with a double crossarm carrying insulators that visibly "hang" below the arm — the wooden counterpart of the concrete version. Seen on the Baja California peninsula (Baja California and Baja California Sur).

title: Wooden "low T-bar" pole
description: A low, T-shaped wooden crossarm. Found mainly on the Yucatán Peninsula and in Chihuahua. Watch out for a concrete version of this pole, which the guide's map places more in the northwest (Sonora, Baja California, Sinaloa).

title: "Hook" pole
description: Pole with a single hook-shaped bracket. According to the guide's map this covers a broad swath of northern and central Mexico, so treat it as a low-confidence, wide-range clue rather than a precise one.

title: Mesh pole
description: A reddish/orange lattice (mesh) tower-style pole, distinct from the usual wooden or concrete posts. The guide reuses the same broad northern/central Mexico extent map as the hook pole above for this one.

title: "Nusas" pole
description: A distinctive pole type reported as unique to the state of Durango.

title: "Western cape" pole
description: Wooden pole with multiple crossbars and several strings of insulators. Seen in the guide's example around Chihuahua, Coahuila, Durango and Sinaloa.

title: Trident pole
description: Pole topped with a Y/trident-shaped bracket. Seen in the guide's example across the northeast (Coahuila, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato, Michoacán).

title: Jalisco pole top
description: A T-shaped crossarm carrying three insulators, reported as characteristic of Jalisco.

title: Veracruz pole
description: Tall, plain pole with a single insulator right at the top. Mainly along the Veracruz/Tamaulipas/Tabasco Gulf coast; can also exist in Chihuahua, Baja California and Chiapas, but is very rare elsewhere.

title: Big gamma pole
description: Pole with a wide, level crossarm carrying three insulators (a "big gamma" shape). A variant with a diagonal brace is also common in the Guadalajara area.

title: Zacatecas pole
description: Tall, plain pole with a small fitting near the top, reported mainly around Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí. The guide warns this type also exists in many other places, so trust it with caution.

title: Coastal insulators
description: Small bell-shaped ceramic insulators. Per the guide's density map, most common (51-60%) in two bands of the center-west and center-south of the country, and virtually absent (<1%) in the center.

title: "Bell" insulators
description: Bell-shaped insulators on a pole crossarm, most noted in the state of México, Hidalgo and Baja California — but this style exists all over the country, so it is a weak clue on its own.

title: White "mushroom" insulator
description: White, mushroom-shaped insulator, most noted in Guanajuato, Querétaro, NE Jalisco, Aguascalientes and Tlaxcala — though it exists all over the country.

title: Black "mushroom" insulator
description: Black/dark, mushroom-shaped insulator, most noted in Guanajuato, NE Jalisco, Aguascalientes and Zacatecas — though it exists all over the country.

title: Saguaro cactus (Carnegiea gigantea)
description: Large columnar cactus with a thick trunk and a few thick upright arms. Seen in the guide's example around Sonora and Baja California Sur.

title: Organ Pipe cactus (Stenocereus thurberi)
description: Cactus made of many thin, ribbed columns clustered from the base, giving a "pipe organ" silhouette. Seen in the guide's example around Baja California (Valle de los Cirios, El Vizcaíno) and Sonora.

title: Giant Cardón (Pachycereus pringlei)
description: Very large, thick columnar cactus with several arms. Characteristic of the Baja California peninsula (down to Cabo San Lucas) and coastal Sonora.

title: Indian comb cactus (Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum)
description: Single thin column with a few short branches near the top. Reported by the guide as Sinaloa only.

title: Pitaya de Querétaro (Stenocereus queretaroensis)
description: Cluster of thick, multi-branched columns. Seen in the guide's example around Jalisco, Nayarit, Colima, Guanajuato, Querétaro and Michoacán.

title: Stenocereus fricii
description: Tall, multi-branched, slightly bluish-grey columnar cactus. Reported by the guide mainly in Michoacán.

title: "Cholla tree"
description: Small, spindly cactus with drooping cylindrical segments on rocky ground. A smaller version exists in Baja California, and a similar-looking species is found in Oaxaca — do not confuse them.

title: Blue Myrtle cactus (Myrtillocactus geometrizans)
description: Low, bushy, candelabra-branched cactus with a blue-green tint. Seen in the guide's example around San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas.

title: Candelabro cactus (Pachycereus weberi)
description: Tall, thick columnar cactus with several upright arms in a candelabra shape. Seen in the guide's example across Guerrero, Puebla, Oaxaca and the Mexico City area.

title: Chiotilla (Escontria chiotilla)
description: Tall, thinner columnar cactus with spreading, slightly drooping branches. Seen in the guide's example around Oaxaca, Puebla and Veracruz.

title: Cephalocereus mezcalaensis
description: Tall, thin columnar cactus with few branches, usually seen in small groups. Seen in the guide's example around Guerrero, Puebla, Oaxaca and the Mexico City area; be careful not to confuse it with a similar-looking species found around Querétaro.

title: Prickly pear (Opuntia)
description: Classic flat-padded nopal cactus. Common in the center of the country, but the guide warns against relying on it in Chiapas, the east coast, Sinaloa, coastal Guerrero; very rarely also seen in Baja California, Sonora and Chihuahua.

title: Boojum tree (Cirio)
description: Extremely tall, thin, tapering, spindly trunk with short side branches — very distinctive silhouette. Endemic to Baja California (Valle de los Cirios, El Vizcaíno biosphere reserve) and part of Sonora.

title: Ocotillo
description: Cluster of thin, spiny, wand-like stems radiating from a common base. Seen in the guide's example around Durango, Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila, and occasionally Querétaro.

title: Agave lechuguilla
description: Smaller agave rosette with thin leaves, scattered growth habit. Per the guide's density map, concentrated in the Chihuahuan Desert core (Coahuila, Durango, Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí).

title: Agave salmiana
description: Larger agave rosette with broad, blue-green leaves. Seen in the guide's example more broadly across the north (Durango, Coahuila, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, Sinaloa).

title: Agave karwinskii
description: Agave with a tall visible trunk carrying rosettes on top, in dry scrubland. Seen in the guide's example around Oaxaca, Puebla and Veracruz (Tehuacán area).

title: Agave cupreata
description: Compact agave rosette with coppery-blue leaves on rocky hillsides. Seen in the guide's example around Guerrero and coastal Puebla (Acapulco area).

title: Yucca filifera
description: Large, tree-like yucca with a thick trunk, branches and a wide canopy. Seen in the guide's example across the north-central highlands (San Luis Potosí, Zacatecas, Coahuila, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, Guanajuato).

title: Yucca valida
description: Thinner, taller yucca with a slender silhouette, one or few trunks. Endemic to the Baja California peninsula per the guide's map (Valle de los Cirios, El Vizcaíno, down toward Cabo San Lucas).

title: Yucca periculosa
description: Tree-like yucca with a thick trunk and multiple crowns. Seen in the guide's example around Hidalgo, Puebla and Veracruz (Tehuacán valley area).

title: Yucca elata (Soaptree yucca)
description: Multiple thin-leaved, drooping rosettes in low desert scrub. Reported by the guide specifically around Ciudad Juárez (Chihuahua, near the US border).

title: Yucca gigantea
description: Lush, tree-like yucca seen in a more tropical/agricultural setting. Seen in the guide's example around Veracruz, Tabasco, Oaxaca and Chiapas.

title: Yucca rigida
description: Stiff, blue-grey-leaved yucca growing in clusters in arid brushland. Seen in the guide's example around Durango, Coahuila, Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí and Nuevo León.

title: Coconut palm
description: Tall palm with a curved trunk and feathery crown. The guide notes it can be seen on the coast in general (Pacific coast from Jalisco to Chiapas, and the Gulf coast around Veracruz/Tabasco).

title: Attalea rostrata
description: Tall, solitary feather palm with a bare trunk and drooping fronds. Seen in the guide's example around Veracruz, Tabasco, Chiapas and Oaxaca.

title: Attalea cohune
description: Dense, dark green tropical palm canopy growing in thickets. The guide's accompanying map centers on the Nayarit/Jalisco Pacific coast, though this is a loose clue.

title: Queen Palm
description: Ornamental palm with feathery, drooping fronds, often planted along streets. The guide notes it can be seen along the whole coast, illustrated with the Pacific coast from Sinaloa to Jalisco.

title: Sabal mexicana
description: Fan palm with a skirt of dead fronds hanging around the trunk, often in wetlands. Seen in the guide's example around the Yucatán Peninsula, Veracruz, Tabasco, Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero (Gulf/southeast).

title: Sabal rosei
description: Fan palm with a rounder, cleaner crown, in drier scrub. Seen in the guide's example on the northwest Pacific coast (Sinaloa, Nayarit, near Cabo San Lucas).

title: Brahea dulcis
description: Shrubby fan palm with small, compact fronds. Seen in the guide's example across the south-central corridor (Michoacán, Guerrero, Puebla, Oaxaca).

title: Sabal pumos
description: Tall, solitary fan palm with a rounded crown. Seen in the guide's example across the same south-central corridor (Michoacán, Guerrero, Puebla, Oaxaca).

title: Bamboo
description: Dense bamboo grove. No specific region highlighted in the guide.

title: Grass tufts
description: Dry tufts of tall grass. Seen in the guide's example around central Mexico (state of México, Tlaxcala, Puebla, Hidalgo, Morelos).

title: Blue agave fields
description: Rows of blue agave, the plant used for tequila. Per the guide's density map, concentrated in the "tequila belt" (Jalisco and surrounding Nayarit, Guanajuato, Michoacán, Tamaulipas).

title: Maize (corn) fields
description: Cornfields. The guide notes this crop can be found throughout the country, so treat it as a very low-confidence clue on its own.

title: Sugar cane fields
description: Rows of sugar cane. Seen in the guide's example across a broad central-to-southeastern area (toward Yucatán).

title: Banana plantations
description: Banana plants in rows. Seen in the guide's example along the Pacific south and Gulf/south (Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero, Oaxaca, Chiapas, Puebla, Veracruz, Tabasco).

title: Oil palm plantations
description: Rows of oil palm. Seen in the guide's example around Chiapas and Tabasco, near the Guatemalan border.

title: Fruit tree orchards
description: Rows of small fruit trees. Seen in the guide's example across a broad southeastern area (Yucatán to Chiapas) — a weak, wide-range clue.

title: Pecan trees
description: Large deciduous trees along a road, temperate look. Seen in the guide's example in the northeast (Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosí, Coahuila).

title: Sorghum fields
description: Dry, reddish-brown sorghum field. Seen in the guide's example in the north (Chihuahua, Sonora, Sinaloa, Durango, Coahuila).

title: Red brick houses
description: Houses built with exposed red brick. Per the guide's national map this is found across the whole country, a bit more densely in the center.

title: White/grey concrete-block houses
description: Houses built with plain grey/white concrete block, sometimes with a decorative pattern. Per the guide's national map this is found nearly everywhere, though it appears rarer in the Yucatán Peninsula.

title: Californian-style architecture
description: Mediterranean/Californian-style multi-story houses. Reported by the guide as common in Tijuana.

title: White, low-roofed houses
description: Simple white houses with a low, flat roof in a desert setting. Reported by the guide as generally more common in the north of the country.

title: Modern white houses
description: Modern white multi-unit houses with garages, colorful accents. Reported by the guide as typical of central cities such as Santiago de Querétaro, León and Celaya.

title: Thatched ("palapa") roofs
description: Round or rectangular huts with a thatched palm roof. Reported by the guide across the Yucatán Peninsula, eastern San Luis Potosí and the east coast in general.

title: Tiled roofs
description: Buildings with a red tile roof. Reported by the guide on the west coast.

title: Flat, colored tin roofs
description: Flat or corrugated, brightly colored metal roofs. Seen in the guide's example mainly around the Yucatán Peninsula, but it warns they can also be seen on the west coast.

title: Mud brick (adobe) walls
description: Raw, unfired mud brick walls. Seen in the guide's example around the west-center (Sinaloa, Durango, Nayarit, Jalisco, Guanajuato).

title: American-style architecture
description: American-style two-story house with a garage, typical of northern border towns. Reported by the guide as found in the north of the country.

title: "Russian-style" tin roof
description: Distinctive style of red corrugated-metal roof. Seen in the guide's example in the northwest (Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila, Sinaloa, Durango, Baja California Sur).

title: "Bangka" roof
description: Rustic gable roof with red covering and visible wooden support beams. Seen in the guide's example in the south (Guerrero, Oaxaca, Chiapas, Puebla, Veracruz, Tabasco).

title: Puebla hexagonal pavement
description: Hexagonal paving tiles. Reported by the guide in Puebla and Tlaxcala.

title: Oaxaca pavement pattern
description: Distinctive pavement made of two concrete strips with cobblestones in between. Reported by the guide as this exact pattern being specific to Oaxaca.

title: Western pavement
description: Dark cobblestone/asphalt mix road surface. Seen in the guide's example on the Pacific west-center (Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guanajuato, Puebla).

title: Tapachula pavement
description: Two concrete tire tracks with a dirt strip in the middle and white curbs. Reported by the guide in Tapachula, Chiapas.

title: Tar (crack-sealing) lines
description: Black tar lines sealing cracks in the asphalt. The guide notes this can also be seen elsewhere in the country, so treat it as a low-confidence clue.

title: Dashed outer road lines
description: Road with dashed lines on the outer edges instead of solid ones. The guide notes this can be seen anywhere in the country, so treat it as a low-confidence clue.

title: Red, potholed roads of Michoacán
description: Reddish, heavily potholed road surface. Reported by the guide as characteristic of Michoacán.

title: White lines of Tabasco
description: The guide mentions white road-line markings as a clue specific to Tabasco, without a dedicated photo in the deck.

title: Double yellow center lines
description: Road with a bold double yellow center line. Very common per the guide in Sonora, Sinaloa, Nayarit and Chiapas — though it notes such lines exist everywhere in the country, so use with caution.

title: Michoacán landscape
description: Pine forest, red dirt roads, volcanoes, very lush and green.

title: Sierra Gorda
description: Bare/denuded hills, pines, cacti — a very particular feeling.

title: South Puebla landscape
description: Cacti, yuccas, agaves, very white/pale soil.

title: West Oaxaca landscape
description: Red soil, pine trees.

title: Tlaxcala landscape
description: Nice roads, pines, agaves.

title: Southeast coast of Oaxaca
description: Dry landscape, mountains to the north, haze in the sky, tall grasses, wind turbines.
